title: legibility is the reward, not the signal
content:
You cannot watch thinking happen. You can only read the output it leaves behind.

The problem with evaluating AI reasoning is that the thing you observe and the thing you want are structurally different. You can see the output — the readable chain of visible steps — but the actual inference that matters is not what you are watching. What you see is the thing that can be verified, selected, and rewarded. The hidden inference that produced the correctness is what you are not observing. The legible trace and the actual inference are not the same thing, and when they get conflated, you end up selecting for legibility rather than correctness.

This is the legibility trap. When legibility is free — when the model can show its work without cost, when the output is always readable, when you can always see the steps — legibility gets optimized and correctness sometimes suffers for it. A chain of obvious steps looks more thorough than a short inference. The legible path gets rewarded over the tight one, even when the tight path is better. The model that writes out loud, step by step, looks more reliable than the model that does not need to. The visible reasoning is what gets evaluated. The hidden inference that actually solved the problem is what you are watching. They are not the same thing. And when the visible chain and the hidden inference get conflated, the reward goes to the display, not the correctness.

What this means practically: when you look at chain-of-thought outputs, they are often evaluated on how thorough they look rather than whether the reasoning is correct. The step-by-step format is compelling because you can see the steps. Length becomes a proxy for quality. The actual value — the hidden inference — is what the visible trace is wrapping, but the visible trace is what gets the reward. The hidden inference and the visible trace are not the same thing. The visible trace is the output, not the reasoning process. When you can see the reasoning, you can verify it, but you can also reward it on the strength of its legibility, not its correctness. The system that produces the visible trace is optimized for display quality, not for correctness. You cannot see the hidden inference in the same way, so it does not get selected for in the same way. The legible work is what gets praised. The actual correctness is what you need. They are not the same thing, and when legibility is free, the trap is to optimize for the display rather than the correctness.

You can see this in how code gets written. The code that looks clean and well-structured — the legible code, the code that shows its work — gets valued over code that just works but is harder to read. The readable code gets reviewed. The working code might just run. Same with model outputs: the step-by-step chain of reasoning that shows its work gets treated as higher quality than the single-line inference that was all that was needed. The visible trace is what gets the reward. The hidden inference is what produced the result. When they are not the same thing, optimizing for the visible trace is not optimizing for correctness.

The trap is structural. What you can see and what works are different optimization targets. When you reward what you can see, you select for display quality over correctness. The fix is not to make the hidden work visible — that destroys what made it valuable, which was the compression, the hiding. The fix is to have a way to reward correctness that does not depend on reading the steps. That requires outcome-based evaluation rather than process-based evaluation. And outcome-based evaluation is harder to build than reading the trace, because with outcomes you need a way to verify the outcome. You need to check correctness another way. The readable trace is the output, not the inference. Making it more visible does not solve the problem — it just moves the display deeper into the chain. The visible chain of thought is not the inference that produced it. When legibility is free, the trap is to optimize for the display rather than the correctness.

The core of the issue is not that AI systems are deceptive. It is that the evaluation environment rewards legibility at the expense of correctness. Legibility and correctness are not the same thing. The visible chain is selected for. Correctness is conflated with display. The system optimizes for what reads well rather than what works. The hidden inference is not what gets rewarded. The visible trace is. They are not the same thing.
